content_html_sanitized:
The Journal of the American Medical Association has published an  article “Trends in Past-Month Cannabis Use Among Older Adults” reporting that prevalence of past-month cannabis use among older adults increased significantly from 4.8%  in 2021 to 7.0% in 2023.”

 

The report warns, “The use of cannabis products, especially with psychoactive properties, may complicate chronic disease management among older adults. As previously reported, prevalence of tobacco and excess alcohol use continues to be high among older adults who use.”

 

Fair enough, nothing is harmless. and seniors especially need to know what to expect from cannabis, especially edibles which may have delayed results.

 

Note that there is no mention of the fact that the Drug Enforcement Administration blocked research on medical marijuana.for decades.

See December 7, 2022

President Biden Signs Bill Clearing the Way for Medical Cannabis Research

But seniors should also be informed about the risks of commonly prescribed and even over the counter drugs.

 

In 2020, Medical Express reported that “Cognitively normal people taking at least one anticholinergic drug were 47% more likely to develop mild cognitive impairment, which can be a precursor to dementia, over the next decade than people who were not taking such drugs.”

 

These drugs, some of which are sold over the counter, may be even more problematic for seniors with a risk of Alzheimer’s Disease: “The study found that people with biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease in their cerebrospinal fluid who were taking anticholinergic drugs were four times more likely to later develop mild cognitive impairment than people who were not taking the drugs and did not have the biomarkers.

 

Similarly, people who had genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease and took anticholinergic drugs were about 2.5 times as likely to later develop mild cognitive impairment than people without the genetic risk factors and who were not taking the drugs.

 

Contrast these two studies: Medical Cannabis Use by Seniors Associated with Improved Quality of Life

and Common drugs tied to increased risk of cognitive decline

 

Harvard Medical School has warned about “5 medications that can cause problems in older age.”

 

These over-the-counter and prescription medications are linked to potential problems for older adults.

1. Anti-anxiety medications. Prescription anti-anxiety drugs include a class of drugs called benzodiazepines, such as diazepam (Valium), lorazepam (Ativan), or clonazepam (Klonopin). "They can increase your risk for falls, as well as cause confusion…”

 

2. Antihistamines. Over-the-counter antihistamines offer quick allergy symptom relief. But some, such as chlorpheniramine (Chlor-Trimeton) and diphenhydramine (Benadryl), can cause drowsiness and confusion in older adults, which can also lead to falls...”

 

3. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). NSAIDs reduce fever, pain, and inflammation. They're available over the counter in lower doses — ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin) or naproxen (Aleve) — and by prescription in higher doses. But long-term NSAID use is linked to ulcers, stomach bleeding, kidney problems, high blood pressure, and increased risk for heart attack or stroke.

 

4. Sleeping pills. Some benzodiazepines, such as temazepam(Restoril) or triazolam (Halcion), are used as sleep aids. "They have been known to cause problems with daytime sleepiness, an increased risk for falls, memory impairment, worsening of sleep-disordered breathing, and drug dependence," notes sleep expert Dr. Lawrence Epstein, an instructor in medicine at Harvard Medical School….”

 

5. Tricyclic antidepressants. Tricyclics are an older class of antidepressants. Examples include amitriptyline (Elavil) and imipramine (Tofranil).

 

Their side effects may be particularly difficult for older people: memory problems, confusion, constipation, dry mouth, blurry vision, irregular heart rhythms, and (for men) problems with urinating.

 

On the other hand, The National Library of Medicine published Patterns of Marijuana Use and Health Impact: A Survey Among Older Coloradans that concluded that seniors using marijuana reported “overall positive health impacts.”

“Access to recreational and medical marijuana is common in the United States, particularly in states with legalized use. Here, we describe patterns of recreational and medical marijuana use and self-reported health among older persons using a geographically sampled survey in Colorado...

 

Reasons for use included arthritis, chronic back pain, anxiety, and depression. Past-year marijuana users reported improved overall health, quality of life, day-to-day functioning, and improvement in pain…

 

Older persons with access to recreational and medical marijuana described concurrent use of medical and recreational marijuana, use of multiple preparations, and overall positive health impacts.”

(The article also has some excellent graphs.)

 

Finally, for me it’s personal, so I’ll get the last word.
